title: A message keeps failing and blocking the queue — how do you handle it?
summary: The classic poison-message question — tests whether you know retry-with-limit plus a dead-letter queue, not just "retry until it works."

slides.markdown:
Infinite retry isn't a safety net here — it's the failure mode itself. A message that can never succeed will retry forever unless something stops it, consuming resources and, on an ordered queue, blocking every message behind it.

The answer the interviewer wants: retry with a limit, then isolate the message in a dead-letter queue instead of retrying it forever.

Ask: **is the failure transient** (a downstream blip that'll clear on its own) **or permanent** (a malformed message that will never succeed)? And: **is this message blocking others behind it, or processing independently?**

The retry-and-DLQ pattern is the same either way, but the urgency changes — a message stalling an ordered partition needs faster isolation than one processing independently.

**Retry with backoff up to a limit**, then **move it to a dead-letter queue** for manual or automated triage instead of retrying forever. The limit is what turns an unbounded failure into a bounded, contained one.

This is the single mechanism that answers both the transient case (a few retries clear it) and the permanent case (it exhausts retries and gets isolated).

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: a max-retry config with an alert on the DLQ
slides.markdown:
A consumer configured with a bounded retry policy and an alert on the dead-letter queue:

```yaml
consumer:
  max_retries: 5
  backoff: exponential   # 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s, 16s
  on_exhausted: dead_letter_queue

alerting:
  dlq_depth_gt: 0
  notify: pagerduty:oncall-messaging
```

A max-retry count of 5 with exponential backoff, then a DLQ with a CloudWatch/Datadog-style alert firing the moment anything lands in it — so triage starts within minutes, not whenever someone happens to check.

A malformed JSON payload from a buggy upstream client fails deserialization every single time. Without a retry limit, it retries forever and, on a FIFO/ordered queue, blocks every message behind it. With a 5-retry cap and a DLQ, it's isolated within seconds and the queue keeps moving.

The blast radius difference is the entire point: unbounded retry turns one bad message into a total outage for that partition; bounded retry contains it to one message.

![DLQ triage runbook: alert, inspect, then fix-and-replay or discard](assets/dlq-triage-runbook.svg)

"Triage" isn't vague here — it's a concrete branch: either the message gets corrected and replayed, or someone documents why dropping it is safe, so nothing sits in the DLQ unaddressed indefinitely.

slides.sectionTitle: The trade-off to name out loud
slides.markdown:
A low retry limit isolates poison messages fast but risks DLQ-ing a message that would have succeeded on, say, the 6th try during a longer transient blip. A high limit rides out longer blips but lets a truly poisoned message block its partition for longer before isolation.

Tune the limit and backoff to the failure patterns you actually observe, not a guess — if downstream outages typically clear within 30 seconds, size the retry window around that instead of an arbitrary count.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: the DLQ is filling up — how do you decide what to do?
slides.markdown:
**Bucket by failure reason** — schema error, downstream timeout, unknown message type — since each bucket has a genuinely different fix, rather than triaging one message at a time as if each were unique.

A DLQ with 200 messages that are all the same schema error is a five-minute fix once identified; triaged one-by-one, it looks like 200 separate incidents.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: can any of the DLQ triage be automated?
slides.markdown:
Yes, for **known failure signatures** — auto-republish on a known-transient error code, for instance — but a **novel failure reason should still page a human** the first time it's seen, rather than silently auto-handling something nobody's classified yet.

Automation for the recognized cases frees people to focus on the genuinely new ones, which is where judgment still matters.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: retrying forever and blocking everything behind it
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "just keep retrying until it eventually works — giving up feels like losing the message."

**Why it's wrong:** on an ordered queue or partition, one bad message that never succeeds blocks every message behind it indefinitely — the queue doesn't just fail to process the bad message, it stalls entirely.

**Correct model:** a bounded retry limit plus a dead-letter queue doesn't lose the message — it's still there, isolated for triage — it just stops that one message from taking the whole partition down with it.

Retry with backoff up to a bounded limit, then move the message to a dead-letter queue instead of retrying forever. Alert immediately on anything landing in the DLQ, bucket failures by reason rather than triaging one-by-one, and automate the known-signature cases while still paging a human on novel failures.

The broader vocabulary for backpressure and dead-letter design this sits inside is covered in [backpressure and dead-letter handling](backpressure-and-dead-letter-handling).
